analysis.one_liner: Directs federal energy regulators to convene a conference on shielding households from AI data center power costs.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee voted 44–0 in July 2026 to advance the bill, which requires a federal conference and report on protecting residential customers from data center energy costs; it still needs a vote by the full House and Senate to become law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill tells the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission — the agency that oversees wholesale electricity markets and transmission — to hold a technical conference within 90 days on strategies and rate structures that protect residential and small-business customers from rising costs tied to very large electricity users like AI data centers. Participants would include utilities, transmission providers, state regulators, ratepayer advocates, and large-load customers such as data centers. Within 180 days after the conference, FERC must report its recommendations to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Energy Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Residential and small commercial electricity customers, especially in regions attracting large data center buildouts, where the cost of new power plants and grid infrastructure can flow through to household bills. Ratepayer advocates gain a formal seat at a federal convening on rate design.

how_it_helps.text: Requires FERC to hold a Commissioner-led technical conference with utilities, transmission providers, state regulators, ratepayer advocates, and large loads including AI data centers on strategies and rate structures for protecting residential and small commercial ratepayers from increased costs associated with large loads [S2].

Requires FERC to submit a report with recommendations and best practices to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee within 180 days of the conference's conclusion [S2].
Puts the question of who pays for data center-driven grid expansion on the formal federal agenda, with ratepayer advocates included among the required participants [S2].

analysis.who_pays: No one bears a direct cost; the expense is a conference and report. The interests most exposed are AI data center operators and large utilities, whose rate structures could face recommendations that shift more infrastructure costs onto large-load customers instead of households — but the bill's recommendations would be non-binding.
analysis.who_pays_short: No direct cost; data centers face scrutiny

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates a conference and a report with recommendations, not any binding rate change; FERC could hold the conference, write the report, and nothing would change on household bills unless FERC or regulators later act [S2].
No deadline or follow-up forces action on the report's recommendations, so critics could fairly call it a study rather than protection.

Rate allocation between large loads and households is complex: shifting costs onto data centers could, in some cases, reduce incentives to locate where grid capacity is plentiful, a tradeoff state economic officials might raise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is minimal — a single federal conference and report. The benefit depends entirely on what comes next: it creates a formal record, gathers regulators and ratepayer advocates, and produces recommendations, but it sets no rate protections itself. It is a first step, not a fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared its House committee unanimously in July 2026 and is waiting for the full House to schedule a vote; nothing has happened yet in the Senate.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the bill on December 9, 2025, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S4].
It gathered 24 cosponsors, 23 Democrats and 1 Republican [S3].
On June 24, 2026, the Energy Subcommittee held a markup and forwarded the bill to the full committee, amended, by voice vote [S4].
On July 21, 2026, the full Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported by a vote of 44 to 0 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost; the bill has bipartisan momentum in the House but no enacted change yet. If it stalls, the current rate structures that let large-load costs flow through to household bills remain untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — bill awaits floor action

sides.party_line_note: The bill has no visible opposition in the record: it advanced unanimously 44–0 in committee and its 24 cosponsors span both parties, though 23 of 24 are Democrats.

industries.industry: AI data centers and large-load energy customers
industries.note: The bill imposes no rules on them, but it convenes a federal process aimed at rate structures that shift more of their infrastructure costs off household bills — a reputational and potential future cost exposure. They are invited participants, not targets, in this version.

Utilities that profit by spreading large-load infrastructure costs across all ratepayers could see recommendations to redesign rates; nothing binding yet. As regulated monopolies, they would remain the channel through which any reform flows.
The bill names ratepayer advocates as required participants in a federal technical conference on protecting residential customers.

analysis.trajectory: A bill ordered reported unanimously by committee typically moves to the House floor, often under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure reserved for noncontroversial bills. With 44–0 committee support and 24 cosponsors, House passage is plausible if leadership schedules it; the open question is whether the Senate takes up a companion before the 119th Congress ends. Many simple oversight bills like this one never get a floor vote despite unanimous committee approval.
